THE EMPLOYEE’S OWN OBLIGATIONS DURING EMPLOYMENT (LAB. CODE §§ 2850–2866; FOLEY V. INTERACTIVE DATA CORP.; TAMENY V. ATLANTIC RICHFIELD CO.; PARATRANSIT, INC. V. UNEMPLOYMENT INS. APPEALS BD.; FERMINO V. FEDCO, INC.; AETNA BUILDING MAINTENANCE CO. V. WEST; KERR’S CATERING SERVICE V. DEPARTMENT OF INDUSTRIAL RELATIONS) — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Lee · Acme, Inc.

PURPOSE AND SCOPE OF THIS INFORMATION SHEET
Acme, Inc. maintains this information sheet to describe what California statutory law says about the obligations an employee owes while employed — the side of the employment relationship that the Labor Code addresses in Article 3 of Chapter 2 of Division 3, headed "Obligations of Employee" and running from section 2850 through section 2866. It is written with reference to the service Jordan Lee performs for Acme, Inc. in the position of Route Service Representative, described for these purposes as servicing the north-county delivery route.

Most of this corpus's During-employment material states what an employer must do or must not do. This sheet states the reciprocal body of statute: the standard of care and skill the Labor Code attaches to service performed for consideration; the duty to comply substantially with the employer's directions and the three exceptions the statute writes into that duty; the duty to perform in conformity with local usage; the duty to prefer the employer's business when the employee has similar business of his or her own; the rule that everything acquired by virtue of the employment belongs to the employer, and the express carve-out for the employee's own compensation; the duties of accounting and of delivery; the rule for an authorized substitute; liability for a culpable degree of negligence; and the rule for service to be rendered jointly.

This sheet describes what the authorities say. It does not evaluate anything Jordan Lee has done or been asked to do, does not determine whether any direction, act or omission satisfies or breaches any of these sections, and does not predict how any court would resolve a dispute.

WHERE THESE DUTIES LIVE IN THE CODE, AND WHERE THEY CAME FROM
The Labor Code divides the general law of the employment relationship into two facing articles. Article 2 of Chapter 2 of Division 3, headed "Obligations of Employer," runs from section 2800 through section 2810.8 and contains the familiar indemnification and reimbursement provisions. Article 3, headed "Obligations of Employee," runs from section 2850 through section 2866. The Legislative Counsel's publication records that both articles were enacted by Statutes of 1937, chapter 90, and that every section of Article 3 quoted in this sheet carries that same enactment note and no later amendment.

The sections are older than 1937. In Foley v. Interactive Data Corp. the California Supreme Court described the 1872 Civil Code as an attempt to codify the common law of master-servant relations and identified the provisions now in the Labor Code as its descendants, quoting section 2854 as an example. In Fermino v. Fedco, Inc. the court gave the pedigree of the obedience provision inside the citation itself, writing "Lab. Code, § 2856 [Civ. Code, former § 1981] et seq."

Foley also recorded what the codification did not settle. The court observed that no enactment expressly requires an employee to report relevant information about other employees to the employer, and said it was not clear whether such a duty is subsumed under the statutory duty of ordinary care or is a separate duty the 1872 Legislature did not codify. That question was left open, and the searches described below located no later California Supreme Court decision answering it.

THE STANDARD OF CARE RISES AND FALLS WITH CONSIDERATION AND BENEFIT; SKILL IS SEPARATELY ADDRESSED
Article 3 does not set a single standard of care. It sets three, graduated by what the person undertaking the service receives and whom the service benefits.

Section 2850 addresses the person who undertakes a service without consideration: that person is not bound to perform at all, but on actually entering upon performance owes at least slight care and diligence. Section 2853 addresses the opposite case, the person employed at his or her own request to do something more for that person's own advantage than for the employer's: that person owes great care and diligence to protect the employer's interest. Section 2854 states the ordinary case of paid employment: one who for a good consideration agrees to serve another shall perform the service and shall use ordinary care and diligence in it, so long as he is thus employed. The closing words of section 2854 mark the duty as one that runs during the employment.

Skill is treated by two further sections rather than folded into the care standard. Section 2858 sets an objective floor — a reasonable degree of skill — but withdraws it where the employer had notice of the employee's want of skill before employing the employee. Section 2859 adds a subjective obligation that has no such exception: the employee is always bound to use such skill as he possesses, so far as it is required for the service specified.

THE DUTY OF OBEDIENCE IS WRITTEN AS SUBSTANTIAL COMPLIANCE WITH THREE EXCEPTIONS
Section 2856 is the provision of Article 3 that California courts cite most often. It is not written as a duty of absolute obedience. It requires substantial compliance with all the employer's directions concerning the service on which the employee is engaged, and it writes three exceptions into the duty itself: obedience that is impossible, obedience that is unlawful, and obedience that would impose new and unreasonable burdens upon the employee.

The California Supreme Court reproduced the section in full in 2014 in Paratransit, Inc. v. Unemployment Ins. Appeals Bd., in a case about whether an employee's refusal to sign a disciplinary notice was misconduct disqualifying him from unemployment benefits. The court set out the employer's argument that any order reasonable in itself triggers the employee's duty of compliance, and concluded that the refusal there was not misconduct but was at most a good faith error in judgment. The opinion decided an unemployment insurance question under section 1256 of the Unemployment Insurance Code; it quoted section 2856 as the statutory backdrop rather than construing the phrase "new and unreasonable burdens."

THE UNLAWFUL-DIRECTION EXCEPTION, AND THE EMPLOYER’S FACING DUTY TO INDEMNIFY
The second exception in section 2856 has carried weight beyond the article. In Tameny v. Atlantic Richfield Co. the California Supreme Court recognized a tort action for discharge in violation of public policy, and pointed to section 2856 as support. The court noted that the earlier decision on which it built had not relied on the section, and said the statute supplied additional support for that ruling. It then stated what the section reflects: although the statute does not speak to the employer's authority to discharge, it reflects direct legislative approval of the proposition that an employer enjoys no authority to direct an employee to engage in unlawful conduct. A separate concurring opinion in Tameny would have rested the cause of action on section 2856 alone.

Article 2 contains the facing provision. Section 2802, subdivision (a), requires the employer to indemnify the employee for all necessary expenditures or losses incurred in direct consequence of the discharge of the employee's duties, or of the employee's obedience to the directions of the employer, "even though unlawful" — unless the employee believed the directions to be unlawful at the time of obeying them. Read alongside section 2856, the two sections address the same event from opposite sides: section 2856 releases the employee from the duty to obey an unlawful direction, and section 2802 places the cost of an obeyed unlawful direction on the employer where the employee did not know it was unlawful.

THE DUTY OF OBEDIENCE DOES NOT REACH THE EMPLOYEE’S PERSON
In Fermino v. Fedco, Inc. the California Supreme Court considered whether an employer's interrogation of an employee suspected of theft could support an action for false imprisonment, or whether it was barred as an ordinary incident of employment. In the course of that analysis the court described an earlier decision in which an employer had argued that no false imprisonment occurred because the employee had received her usual compensation for the time she was held, and was therefore merely performing an employment-related service during that time. The court recorded that the argument had been rejected: the statutory and implied contractual provisions requiring an employee to follow an employer's directions — the court cited section 2856 and the sections following it, with the 1872 Civil Code ancestor in brackets — do not authorize the employer forcibly to detain the employee's person in order to compel a confession of an earlier theft of the employer's property.

The passage marks a boundary that the text of section 2856 states only in general terms. It identifies a category of employer direction that the duty of substantial compliance does not reach at all, independently of whether the direction is characterized as impossible, as unlawful, or as a new and unreasonable burden.

PERFORMANCE MUST CONFORM TO THE USAGE OF THE PLACE, SUBJECT TO TWO OVERRIDES
Section 2857 supplies a default rule of performance drawn from custom rather than from the contract. The employee is to perform the service in conformity to the usage of the place of performance. The section then states two things that displace the usage: a contrary direction from the employer, and impracticability or manifest injury to the employer.

The structure is worth setting beside section 2856. Section 2856 makes the employer's direction the primary source of the employee's obligation and says nothing about usage; section 2857 makes usage the default and the employer's direction the override. The two sections describe the same relationship from different starting points, and the article does not state which governs where they point in different directions.

Acme, Inc. maintains this information sheet to describe what California statutory law says about the obligations an employee owes while employed — the side of the employment relationship that the Labor Code addresses in Article 3 of Chapter 2 of Division 3, headed "Obligations of Employee" and running from section 2850 through section 2866. It is written with reference to the service Jordan Lee performs for Acme, Inc. in the position of Route Service Representative, described for these purposes as servicing the north-county delivery route.

Most of this corpus's During-employment material states what an employer must do or must not do. This sheet states the reciprocal body of statute: the standard of care and skill the Labor Code attaches to service performed for consideration; the duty to comply substantially with the employer's directions and the three exceptions the statute writes into that duty; the duty to perform in conformity with local usage; the duty to prefer the employer's business when the employee has similar business of his or her own; the rule that everything acquired by virtue of the employment belongs to the employer, and the express carve-out for the employee's own compensation; the duties of accounting and of delivery; the rule for an authorized substitute; liability for a culpable degree of negligence; and the rule for service to be rendered jointly.

This sheet describes what the authorities say. It does not evaluate anything Jordan Lee has done or been asked to do, does not determine whether any direction, act or omission satisfies or breaches any of these sections, and does not predict how any court would resolve a dispute.

The Labor Code divides the general law of the employment relationship into two facing articles. Article 2 of Chapter 2 of Division 3, headed "Obligations of Employer," runs from section 2800 through section 2810.8 and contains the familiar indemnification and reimbursement provisions. Article 3, headed "Obligations of Employee," runs from section 2850 through section 2866. The Legislative Counsel's publication records that both articles were enacted by Statutes of 1937, chapter 90, and that every section of Article 3 quoted in this sheet carries that same enactment note and no later amendment.

The sections are older than 1937. In Foley v. Interactive Data Corp. the California Supreme Court described the 1872 Civil Code as an attempt to codify the common law of master-servant relations and identified the provisions now in the Labor Code as its descendants, quoting section 2854 as an example. In Fermino v. Fedco, Inc. the court gave the pedigree of the obedience provision inside the citation itself, writing "Lab. Code, § 2856 [Civ. Code, former § 1981] et seq."

The court observed that no enactment expressly requires an employee to report relevant information about other employees to the employer, and said it was not clear whether such a duty is subsumed under the statutory duty of ordinary care or is a separate duty the 1872 Legislature did not codify. That question was left open, and the searches described below located no later California Supreme Court decision answering it.

No enactment expressly requires an employee to report relevant information concerning other employees to his employer, and none prohibits discharge of the employee for so doing.

Article 3 does not set a single standard of care. It sets three, graduated by what the person undertaking the service receives and whom the service benefits.

Section 2850 addresses the person who undertakes a service without consideration: that person is not bound to perform at all, but on actually entering upon performance owes at least slight care and diligence. Section 2853 addresses the opposite case, the person employed at his or her own request to do something more for that person's own advantage than for the employer's: that person owes great care and diligence to protect the employer's interest. Section 2854 states the ordinary case of paid employment: one who for a good consideration agrees to serve another shall perform the service and shall use ordinary care and diligence in it, so long as he is thus employed. The closing words of section 2854 mark the duty as one that runs during the employment.

Skill is treated by two further sections rather than folded into the care standard. Section 2858 sets an objective floor — a reasonable degree of skill — but withdraws it where the employer had notice of the employee's want of skill before employing the employee. Section 2859 adds a subjective obligation that has no such exception: the employee is always bound to use such skill as he possesses, so far as it is required for the service specified.

The exception written into section 2860 for "the compensation which is due to him from his employer" has been given weight by the California Supreme Court. In Kerr's Catering Service v. Department of Industrial Relations the court considered an employer's practice of deducting cash shortages from the wages of its route employees. Quoting section 2860 in abbreviated form with the compensation clause italicized, the court said it is manifest that wages due belong to the employee and not to the employer. In the same passage the court observed that it is doubtful an employer holding an unliquidated damages claim against an employee would be permitted to withhold wages that the employer could not reach as a judgment creditor.

Both propositions bear on the rest of Article 3. The duties Article 3 imposes on the employee are duties owed to the employer, and section 2865 makes a culpably negligent employee liable to the employer for the resulting damage. Kerr's Catering addresses what an employer may do about such a claim while wages are due: it places the wages on the employee's side of section 2860's line.

Four sections of Article 3 deal with the mechanics of the relationship rather than with standards of conduct.

Section 2861 states two duties of account. On demand, the employee is to render just accounts of all transactions in the course of the service, as often as is reasonable. Without demand, the employee is to give prompt notice of everything received for the employer's account. The first duty is triggered by a demand; the second is not.

Section 2862 addresses delivery of what has been received, and it runs in the employee's favour. An employee who receives something on the employer's account in any capacity other than that of a mere servant is not bound to deliver it until it is demanded, and is not at liberty to send it from a distance, without demand, in any mode involving greater risk than keeping it.

Section 2864 addresses the employee who is expressly authorized to employ a substitute. That employee is liable to the principal only for want of ordinary care in selecting the substitute, and the substitute is directly responsible to the principal.

Section 2866 addresses service to be rendered jointly by two or more persons where one of them dies. The survivor is to act alone if the service is such as he can rightly perform without the aid of the deceased person, but not otherwise.

Section 2865 is the one provision of Article 3 that states a money liability running from the employee to the employer. An employee guilty of a culpable degree of negligence is liable to the employer for the damage thereby caused. The section's second sentence runs the other way: where the service is not gratuitous, the employer is liable to the employee for the value of only such services as are properly rendered.

The California Supreme Court described the right of action in County of San Diego v. Rogge that no case had been found or cited defining the phrase as the section sets it out. The Court of Appeal returned to section 2865 in Nicholas Laboratories v. Chen, where it listed negligence under the section among the grounds on which an employer may sue an employee, and held that Labor Code section 2802 did not require the employer to indemnify the employee's attorney fees incurred in defending the employer's own suit.
